title: Capacity Safeguard Orchestration and Tenant Fencing
creator: Aisha Kumar
description: PRD for an orchestration layer that enforces headroom, soft-fencing, and predictable degradation across reserved pools. Introduces the Capacity Safeguard ("safety mesh") concept: a policy plane that coordinates reserved pool headroom, tenant fencing decisions, burst credit accounting, and observable eviction/recovery behavior for Dedicated capacity customers.
problem_statement: Large tenants with reserved pools occasionally cause noisy neighbors and hotspots during bursts. Current reserve semantics either overcommit or force hard evictions that break SLAs. We need an orchestration and fencing layer to provide: (1) predictable degradation for low-priority workloads, (2) transparent burst accounting, and (3) automated soft-preemption so critical latency targets are preserved for high-priority tenants.
goals: Provide a policy engine ('safety mesh') that maintains configurable headroom per reserved pool and triggers graceful degradation rules when headroom is exhausted.
Implement tenant fencing: ordered, auditable soft-preemption handshake between scheduler and tenant runtime to reclaim capacity without hard-killing requests.
Expose burst credit and escrow ledger per tenant so burst usage is visible, billable, and pluggable into quota decisions.
Reduce P99 latency violations under contention by 60% for high-SLA tenants compared to current baseline.
Ship admin and tenant-facing observability: per-tenant headroom, credit balance, eviction traces, and 'why-waiting' reasons in Console and APIs.
non_goals: Re-architect the serving runtime kernels or implement low-level GPU preemption (this is orchestration and policy only).
Replace existing dedicated billing model—billing integration will be follow-up work.
Support on-prem air-gapped installs in the initial iteration; plan for next-phase Private release.
success_metrics: High-SLA tenants: P99 latency regressions under contention <= +5% vs baseline within 2 weeks of rollout.
Reduction of hard-eviction events by >= 80% in production cluster during test floods.
Operator churn: mean time to diagnose a contention event reduced from 3 hours to 30 minutes using new telemetry dashboards.
Adoption: at least 3 strategic Dedicated customers opt into safety-mesh beta within quarter.
requirements: Policy configuration: headroom percentage or absolute vGPU/sec per reserved pool, priority classes, and graceful-degrade rules (throttle, defer, preempt-with-grace).
Fencing handshake: an RPC contract between scheduler and tenant agent to request voluntary slowdown with timeout and escalation path to soft-evict.
Burst credit ledger: per-tenant credit accounting with accrual rate, cap, and emergency-credit option for SRE-controlled grants.
Observability: Console panel and API endpoints for headroom, credit balance, current degradations, and recent fencing events (timestamped traces, related allocations).
Auditability: every change to policy or forced reclaim must create an immutable audit event with reason, actor, and related allocations.
Rollback safety: ability to revert safety-mesh behavior to 'pass-through' mode per-zone within 5 minutes.
detailed_spec:
Overview:
The safety mesh runs as a control-plane component that subscribes to current pool allocations and real-time telemetry (utilization, queuing, per-tenant latencies). It enforces headroom by maintaining a sliding capacity budget per pool and issues 'fence' requests when projected consumption exceeds headroom thresholds.

Headroom orchestration:
- Config model: pools have headroom configured as either percentage (e.g., 15%) or absolute units. The mesh continuously projects 1-minute and 5-minute consumption and reserves the headroom budget.
- If projected consumption > (available - headroom), the mesh selects victims using priority classes, last-recent-burst, and recent error impact history.

Tenant fencing handshake:
- Fence RPC: send {tenant_id, target_reduction_pct, grace_seconds, reason, correlation_id}. Tenant agent responds with: {ack, estimated_quiesce_time}.
- If ack within grpc_timeout, scheduler applies soft-throttles (token-bucket reductions, queue-length caps) and marks allocation as 'fenced'.
- If no ack or ack > grace_seconds, escalate to 'soft-evict' which pauses new request acceptance and drains existing low-priority connections. Soft-evict is observable and reversible.

Burst credit ledger:
- Accrual model: credits accrue at config rate per tenant based on committed capacity and past usage patterns.
acceptance_criteria: Policy configuration UI in Console that allows creating/updating headroom and degrade rules for a reserved pool.
Fence RPC implemented and end-to-ended in staging with a mock tenant agent that honors reduce/ack/timeout semantics.
Automated test harness that simulates multi-tenant bursts and demonstrates >80% reduction in hard-evictions vs baseline.
API endpoint /v1/dedicated/pools/{pool_id}/headroom and /v1/dedicated/tenants/{tenant_id}/credits returning current state.
Audit log events emitted for each fencing decision and retained in Console for 90 days (configurable).
Rollback: a zone-level feature flag that sets safety-mesh to pass-through must revert behavior within 5 minutes in staging and production canary.
rollout_plan: Phase 1 (staging): deploy mesh in passive mode (read-only) for 2 weeks; collect telemetry and tune projection windows. Phase 2 (canary): enable active mode for non-critical pools (10% of capacity) and test fencing handshake with synthetic tenants. Phase 3 (beta): opt-in beta customers in a dedicated region; expose Console controls. Phase 4 (general): enable by default with conservative defaults and 1-week observation window before expanding. Each phase includes chaos tests: sudden 5x burst, region failover, and slow tenant agent responses.
dependencies_field: Tenant agent runtime: support for fence RPC (ENG-802)
Console: headroom UI and audit viewer (ENG-1203)
stakeholders: SRE Team: incident playbooks and canary ops
risks: Tenant agents may not be able to quiesce quickly—risk of increased tail latency if fencing fails.
Overly aggressive headroom settings could waste capacity and increase cost for customers.
Complexity of credit ledger billing integration may delay GA features.
open_questions: What is the authoritative owner of credit ledger for billing—Platform billing or Dedicated metering service?
What default headroom percent should we ship with for multi-tenant pools? (propose 12% but need SRE calibration)
How should cross-zone preemption work for workloads pinned to a zone?
links: Related PRD: PM-273911 (predictive-buffering and fairburst policy)
notes: We should coordinate an early workshop with 3 customers who experienced hard evictions last quarter. Draft SLO targets with SRE before canary. Keep the initial UI minimal: toggle + sliders for headroom and priority classes.
